To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
B7‐2‐/– female NOD mice develop a spontaneous neuropathy that is mediated by B cells, and that regulatory B and T cells control the development and severity of the neuropathy.
B7‐2 deficiency in NOD mice leads to a lower frequency of Bregs and a lower number of Tregs, which results in an exacerbated autoimmune polyneuromyelitis that mimics CIDP.

Bregs and B7‐2+ Tregs control the development and progression of autoimmune polyneuromyelitis in a non‐overlapping and non‐reducing fashion, and that B cell‐deficiency prevents the disease development in this model.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development and progression of a spontaneous autoimmune disease of the nervous system in a mouse model.
the role of B cells, B cell subsets (including Bregs), and Tregs in the immunopathogenesis of a spontaneous model of chronic inflammatory demye‐linating polyradiculonewopathy (CIDP).
the pathophysiology and treatment of autoimmune neuropathies, such as CIDP, and we have developed a spontaneous animal model of the disease that mimics the human condition.

the B7‐2 molecule is critical for the maintenance of the balance between Treg and Breg cells, and the loss of this balance results in the development of an autoimmune polyneuromyopathy.

B7‐2 is a critical molecule in the generation and maintenance of regulatory T and B lymphocyte populations in NOD mice and that these cells are essential in controlling the development and progression of the autoimmune polyneuporathy in these mice.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the regulatory role of B cells in the development of autoimmune disease is more prominent than their effector role, which is in contrast to what has been reported for T cells.
Bregs and regulatory T cells are important in controlling the immunopathogenesis of an autoimmune model of CIDP.
the B cell‐deficiency model is the most effective way to prevent SAP in B7‐2‐deficient NOD mice and that the regulatory B cells are the most important in the control of SAP.
